title: Ops-to-Sales Incident Narrative Templates and Regional Fallback Positioning
content:
Purpose:
This working brief is intended to give go-to-market (sales, AMs, and pre-sales) a concise set of incident narratives, regional fallback positioning, and competitive call-outs that map to real operational controls. Use these as templates for customer conversations, renewal decks, and battlecards.

Audience:
- Sales reps and AEs
- Solutions engineers and CSMs
- GTM leadership preparing public messaging or enterprise renewals

What this doc is (and isn’t):
- It’s a practical script / template library and one-page competitive posture for reliability and graceful degradation.
- Not a full runbook for SREs—link to infra runbooks for technical detail.

Core positioning pillars (short):
1) Predictable availability: SLAs and reserved capacity options mean customers can choose a deterministic behavior profile (hosted -> dedicated -> private).
2) Controlled degradation: When partial capacity constraints happen, Redwood prefers graceful, customer-configurable fallbacks over opaque failures.
3) Transparent trust signals: clear upstream signals, post-incident summaries, and verifiable failover behaviours.
4) Economic continuity: fallbacks are designed to preserve value (e.g., lower-cost variant or cached responses) rather than severing service.

Fallback taxonomy (one-liner descriptions):
- Regional failover: automatic routing to warm-region pools with same model variant or compatible substitute.
- Model-slim fallback: degrade to a quantized/finite-context variant to preserve latency and throughput.
- Cached prefix responses: serve cached completions for repeat prefixes during short outages.
- Queue-then-burst: place non-latency-sensitive requests into a short queue and process when capacity resumes.
- API-level soft-degradation: return structured partial results + explicit status so apps can handle partial outputs.

How to explain to customers (3-tier messaging):
- Quick explain (30s): "We design for continuity — if a region or model experiences pressure, we automatically switch to verified fallbacks that keep your feature responding, often with slightly lower throughput or a compact model, rather than returning errors."
- Mid-length (2-3 min): highlight options (Dedicated reserved capacity, Private deployments, and policy-level fallback controls), and an example: "During a cap spike in us-west, we routed to us-east warm pools; customer-visible latency rose 60ms and tokens used switched to a quantized variant with identical prompt/response semantics for core tasks."
- Technical (team call): show the fallback matrix, SLA/latency numbers, and the observability footprint (traces, token-count deltas, rollback button).

Incident narrative templates (editable snippets):
1) Initial customer alert (public-friendly):
"We’re experiencing degraded inference performance across a subset of requests in US-West. Our platform has initiated our fallback policy—requests are being routed through healthy regions and compatible model variants. You may see a small increase in latency and occasional shorter responses. Our teams are actively investigating. We’ll post an update in 30 minutes with impact and ETA."

2) Mid-incident customer update (operational):
"Update: Root cause appears to be a capacity surge tied to an upstream client pattern plus a driver-level kernel regression on a subset of GPU instances. We’ve mitigated by shifting affected workloads to dedicated warm pools in another region and activating a model-slim fallback for non-critical routes. Error rates have dropped from 3.2% to 0.4% since the mitigation. We estimate reduced residual impact for the next 90 minutes while we stabilize autoscaling thresholds and rollout a kernel patch."

3) Post-incident narrative (postmortem summary for customers):
"Summary: On 2026-03-10, a capacity surge plus a rare instance-level performance regression increased inference errors and latency for some customers. Impact: transient errors and slower responses for ~4% of requests for 42 minutes. Mitigations: regional failover to warm pools, model-slim fallbacks for non-latency-critical routes, and token-caching. Outcome: systems returned to normal after autoscaling adjustments and patch rollout. Action items: limit-one pattern to throttling rules, additional warm pool capacity for high-traffic tenants, and improved signal for early autoscaling triggers. If you prefer we can schedule account-specific resilience tuning (reserved capacity or private deployment) as a follow-up."

Trust language and contrast vs. competitors (talking points):
- We favor explicit, customer-configurable fallback policies. Competitor A tends to auto-retry without structured partial results which can hide failures; Competitor B has a single-region execution model in some tiers.
- Talk about transparency: "We expose token-level cost/latency deltas during fallback. That means you can audit whether a fallback increased cost or shortened output length."
- Differentiator: unified controls across hosted/dedicated/private — customers can use the same fallback policy even as they migrate.

Sales objection handling (examples):
- "I don’t want silent quality drops": "Agree — silent drops are bad. With Redwood, fallbacks are explicit and include a response flag and optional confidence score so your app can present or fallback gracefully. We can expose those flags to your devs immediately via the SDK."
- "Multi-region seems expensive": "We use warm pools and pre-authorized capacity policies to keep cross-region reserves cost-effective; Dedicated customers can set burst policies to limit cross-region spend while guaranteeing continuity."
- "How do I prove this works?": "We can run a chaos/resilience test on your staging traffic (short, controlled) and provide metrics and video of failover behavior. We also provide per-route canary configs for gradual rollout."

Competitive analysis notes (short bullets for battlecards):
- Cloud-hosted LLM endpoints: often simpler but limited in fallbacks and observability. Price/latency unknowns during outages.
- LLM API incumbents: strong brand but variable degradations; some use opaque autoscaling that returns errors instead of degraded but useful responses.
- Inference infra vendors (self-host): give total control but require ops investment. Redwood: middle ground — managed runtime with enterprise-grade fallback controls.

Operational hooks GTM should know (what ops does, so sales can speak credibly):
- We maintain per-tenant warm pools by region and model family; failover is warmed to a consistent model family, not an arbitrary variant.
- Model-slim fallbacks preserve prompt semantics for core intents (NER/classification) but may truncate creative generation.
- Structured fallback flags (x-redwood-fallback: true; fallback-variant: quantized-16) are emitted to customers’ request logs.
- Observable metrics available to customers: per-route token delta, latency percentile before/after fallback, and fallback incidence.

Suggested collateral updates (short list):
- Renewal slide: single slide showing 3 fallback modes + customer-visible signals and what happens to latency and token cost.
- One-pager for AMs: table of common objections + TL;DR responses + an offer to run a resilience demo.
- Engineer-facing Playbook: link to infra runbook and a short checklist for the SE to run a staging failover test with the customer.

Example short scripts for customer calls (pick-one):
- For worried execs: "We architected Redwood so your app keeps serving — when pressure hits we switch to verified fallbacks with transparent indicators. If you want, we can quantify this for your workload in a 1-hour test."
- For dev leads: "We’ll expose a fallback flag and a dedicated telemetry stream you can wire into your monitoring; we can also configure route-level policies to prefer cost or latency during fallback."

Next steps / open questions (internal):
- Finalize one-pager for CSMs and AMs by 2026-03-20.
- Request sample telemetry from engineering showing the exact header names and example traces for inclusion in collateral.
- Decide whether to add a customer-facing SLA addendum specifically describing fallback behaviour.

Notes / scratch area (things to refine next pass):
- Add a compact diagram showing routing path during regional failover.
- Concrete numbers for latency and token-cost deltas per model family to include in renewal slides.
- Consider a short customer case study for a recent outage (redacted) showing the benefit of our fallbacks.
